title: Practice: min/max of three & character classes
overview: Two classic beginner problems, solved cleanly with if / else-if ladders: find the smallest and largest of three numbers, and decide whether a character is a digit, a capital letter or a small letter. These are improved versions of the Book/Module2 exercises.

concepts.term: Store the answer in a variable
concepts.explain: Set `min` and `max` inside the ladders, then print once at the end. This is cleaner than printing inside every branch.
Digits are 48–57, capital letters 65–90 and small letters 97–122. Compare against the character literals (`'0'`, `'A'`, `'a'`) instead of memorising the numbers.
Judges compare output character by character, so match the task's spaces and line breaks exactly.

files.title: Max and Min of three

problem.name: Codeforces group - K. Max and Min

files.what: Finds the minimum and maximum of A, B and C with two else-if ladders and prints `min max`.
steps: Maximum: if `a` is at least as big as both others, `max = a`. Otherwise check `b`. Otherwise `max = c`.
Print `min max` separated by one space.
files.output_note: The smallest value is -5 and the largest is 20, so it prints `-5 20`.

check.q: Using the variable names `a`, `b`, `c`, how could you shorten the max ladder?
check.a: Start with `max = a;`, then `if (b > max) max = b; if (c > max) max = c;`.

files.title: Capital or Small or Digit

problem.name: Codeforces group - M. Capital or Small or Digit

files.what: Prints `IS DIGIT` for a digit. For a letter, it prints `ALPHA` and then whether the letter is capital or small.
steps: If `ch` is between '0' and '9', print `IS DIGIT`.
Else if it is between 'A' and 'Z', print `ALPHA` and `IS CAPITAL` on two lines.
Else if it is between 'a' and 'z', print `ALPHA` and `IS SMALL`.
files.output_note: For `a` it prints `ALPHA` and then `IS SMALL`. Unlike the Book version, the edge letter `a` is handled correctly.

check.q: What is the ASCII value of '0', and why don't we need to remember it?
check.a: 48. Writing `'0'` in the code means the compiler fills in the number for us.

practice_links.name: M. Capital or Small or Digit

recap: Keep the result in `min`/`max` variables and print once.
Test character classes with inclusive ranges on character literals.
Match the judge's output format exactly.

check_yourself.q: How would you find the maximum of three numbers with only two `if` statements (no `else`)?
check_yourself.a: `max = a; if (b > max) max = b; if (c > max) max = c;`

check_yourself.q: Convert a digit character `ch` to its number value.

check_yourself.a: Yes. 90 < 97; all capital letters come before the small letters in ASCII.

body: Two old friends today, done properly. Put three cards face up on a table - say 10, 20 and -5 - and you see the smallest and the largest in one glance. A computer cannot glance. It can only ask one yes/no question at a time, and each question compares two values.
So the job is to turn one glance into a short list of comparisons, using nothing but the `if` / `else if` ladder from Module 02.

The clumsy way is to work out which of the six possible orders you are in and print inside each branch. Six branches, six `printf`s, and if the task later wants the two numbers on separate lines you have to edit all six.
The tidy way is to decide what to **remember**, not what to print. Set a variable, then print once at the end:

This is the small shift compared with the earlier modules. Until now an `if` chose which line to print; here it chooses which value to keep, and the printing is one line at the very end. Change the output format later and you change that one line.
Follow the cards 10, 20 and -5 through both ladders:
intro.trace:
a = 10    b = 20    c = -5
max:  a>=b ?  10>=20  no   -> try b
      b>=a and b>=c ?  yes -> max = 20
min:  a<=b and a<=c ?  no  -> try b
      b<=a ?  20<=10  no   -> else, min = -5
prints:  -5 20

body: Watch the `>=` rather than `>`. Suppose the values are 5, 5 and 1. With `a > b && a > c` the first test fails because 5 is not greater than 5, the second fails for the same reason, and the `else` hands you `c`, which is 1. The answer would be plainly wrong. Ties are normal in test data, so write the comparisons so that a tie still picks a correct value. A shorter form avoids the trap altogether: `max = a; if (b > max) max = b; if (c > max) max = c;`

**The second problem, from another angle.** You are handed one character and must say whether it is a digit, a capital letter or a small letter. A `char` is really a small number - `'0'` is 48, `'A'` is 65, `'a'` is 97 - and the three groups sit in unbroken blocks, so "is it a digit" is just "is it inside the block": `ch >= '0' && ch <= '9'`. Write the characters, not the numbers, and the compiler fills in 48 and 57 for you. Both ends are included, so `'0'` and `'9'` are digits, and `'a'` and `'z'` are small letters.
intro.trace:
ch    digit?   capital?   small?   output
'7'    yes        -         -      IS DIGIT
'K'     no       yes        -      ALPHA
                                   IS CAPITAL
'a'     no        no       yes     ALPHA
                                   IS SMALL

body: Why practise such small problems? Because picking one value out of several, and sorting a character into a class, turn up inside almost every larger program you will write, and both are places where a careless boundary quietly costs you a correct answer. The edge cases here are exactly the boundaries: equal values, and the first and last letter of a block.

The last thing to get right is the output itself. A judge compares your text character by character, so `min` comes first, one space between the two numbers, and `ALPHA` sits on its own line above `IS CAPITAL`. The two programs below show both, with the boundary cases handled.
